study_identification.title: Normative modelling of molecular-based functional circuits captures clinical heterogeneity transdiagnostically in psychiatric patients

study_characteristics.study_objective: To integrate REACT (Receptor-Enriched Analysis of functional Connectivity by Targets) with normative modeling to characterize individual-level deviations in molecular-enriched functional networks across psychiatric disorders. The study aimed to link transdiagnostic symptomatology to molecular and systems-level brain dysfunction spanning schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and ADHD.

hc_age.answer: CamCAN: mean 52.3 (SD 18.3), age range 18-87 years; UCLA: mean 31.2 (SD 8.7), age range 21-50 years

preprocessing_pipeline.answer: fMRIPrep v20.2.5; ANTs for spatial normalization to MNI152NLin6Asym; MCFLIRT for motion correction; ICA-AROMA for automatic motion artifact removal; field map correction (CamCAN only); custom combination of atlases: Schaefer 400 cortical parcellation, Harvard-Oxford subcortical (15 regions), SUIT cerebellar (28 regions) for total 443 ROIs

quality_checking_detail.answer: Visual inspection of all fMRIprep quality control images and metrics for every subject. Exclusion criteria: head motion exceeding 0.5mm framewise displacement; significant dropout in front-temporal regions; repeated registration failures. Following quality control exclusions, 607 healthy subjects and 119 patients were included in final analysis.

site_effect_handling_detail.answer: Hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) with site (UCLA, CamCAN) modeled as random effects and age and sex as fixed effects. The HBR approach accommodates signal and noise variance in data from multiple sites by estimating different but connected mean and variance components through shared prior distributions across sites.

response_variable.answer: Molecular-enriched functional connectivity (FC) values for 6 systems: noradrenergic (NAT), dopaminergic (DAT), serotonergic (SERT), cholinergic (VAChT), glutamatergic (mGluR5), and GABAergic (GABA-A) networks across 443 ROIs

predictor_effects.answer: Site (UCLA, CamCAN) = random effect; Age and Sex = fixed effects. HBR models were trained separately for each ROI and each receptor system.

nm_vldtn_handle_ns.reason: The study explicitly addresses nuisance structure through multiple mechanisms: (1) Hierarchical Bayesian regression framework that models site-specific variance through random effects with shared prior distributions, accommodating both mean and variance differences across sites; (2) Motion handling through exclusion criteria (>0.5mm framewise displacement) and ICA-AROMA for automatic artifact removal; (3) Quality control procedures including visual inspection and exclusion of subjects with registration failures or signal dropout; (4) Age and sex are modeled as fixed effects to account for their systematic effects; (5) The VIF analysis confirmed acceptable collinearity levels (<5) between molecular templates in the REACT framework.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.supporting_text: We chose to utilise a hierarchical Bayesian regression (HBR) approach which can accommodate signal and noise variance in data from multiple sites by estimating different but connected mean and variance components through shared prior distributions across sites. Specifically, we used site (UCLA, Cambridge) as a random effect as well as age and sex as fixed effects, resulting in normative regional molecular-enriched FC variance and uncertainty. [...] Participants with head motion exceeding 0.5mm framewise displacement were excluded. [...] ICA-AROMA was performed [...] VIF values between the different molecular templates were also moderate, but importantly not surpassing the rule-of-thumb value of 5 above which issues of collinearity are considered sufficiently high to warrant additional consideration.
nm_vldtn_handle_ns.location: Main text Methods section 6.6 (Normative modelling); Supplementary methods (Imaging pre-processing)

nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.reason: The study employed a 70/30 train-test split of the healthy control data from both UCLA and CamCAN datasets. The training set (70%) was used to build normative models, and the test set (30%) from the same datasets was used to evaluate model performance. This represents validation on non-independent data within the same domain as the data comes from the same source datasets, though temporally separated. Model performance was quantified using explained variance (EV), with results showing moderate EV that varied substantially between molecular-enriched networks and across ROIs. Only regions with positive EV were retained for subsequent analyses.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.supporting_text: Normative models were trained on 70% of the healthy control data across both UCLA and CamCAN datasets and tested on the remaining 30%. These trained models explained a moderate amount of variance (EV) in molecular-enriched networks in this unseen data using age and sex as predictor variables. This EV varied substantially between molecular enriched-networks and across ROIs (SI-Fig. 4). Herein, all analyses utilise only regions that had positive EV for that receptor system (from the total of 443 regions, this was 319, 307, 296, 257, 418, and 421 for NAT, DAT, SERT, VAChT, mGluR5, and GABA-A respectively).
nm_vldtn_same_domain_nonindep.location: Main text Results section 2.5 (Modelling the normative molecular-enriched brain); Methods section 6.6

nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.reason: While the study used a train-test split within the same datasets (CamCAN and UCLA), there is no evidence of validation using completely independent healthy control samples from different datasets or cohorts not involved in the training process. The test set (30% of HC from CamCAN and UCLA) is derived from the same source datasets as the training set, making it non-independent in terms of data source, though it is held-out data. True independent same-domain validation would require testing on healthy controls from entirely separate cohorts not used in model development.
nm_vldtn_same_domain_indep.supporting_text: No explicit mention of validation on completely independent healthy control cohorts from different sources.

nm_vldtn_diff_domain.reason: The study applies the normative models trained on healthy controls to clinical populations (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and ADHD), which could be considered different-domain validation in terms of population characteristics. The models successfully identified deviations in clinical groups, with significant differences found between patients and controls for certain molecular systems. However, this is not validation in the traditional sense of testing model generalizability across different scanning sites, protocols, or geographical locations that were not part of the training data. The clinical application serves more as a use-case demonstration rather than a formal validation of model generalizability across different domains.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.supporting_text: From the UCLA dataset, a total of 119 patients was used in the final analysis, including patients suffering from SCHZ (N=38, Mean age (SD) = 35.1 (8.8), M/F = 32/6), BPD (N=44, Mean age (SD) = 34.6 (8.9), M/F = 24/22), and ADHD (N=37, Mean age (SD) = 32.2 (10.1), M/F = 19/18). [...] The tests revealed statistically significant differences within the VAChT and mGluR5 systems. [...] Summary deviation metrics that showed significant differences in lower-level comparisons were then used within a binary logistic regression, which revealed a moderate capacity to discriminate patients with SCHZ and BPD from healthy controls.
nm_vldtn_diff_domain.location: Main text Results sections 2.1 (Demographics), 2.6 (Comparing deviations from normality across conventional diagnostic groups)

diseases_studied.answer: Schizophrenia (SCHZ); Bipolar Disorder (BPD); Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)

clinical_groups_age.answer: SCHZ: mean 35.1 (SD 8.8); BPD: mean 34.6 (SD 8.9); ADHD: mean 32.2 (SD 10.1)

deviation_metric.answer: Z-score based deviation scores (one deviation value per ROI, subject, and molecular system). Positive deviations indicate molecular-enriched FC greater than normal population ranges; negative deviations indicate FC lower than normal ranges. Mean deviation scores across ROIs were also computed as summary metrics for each subject and molecular system.

clinical_application_and_analysis.association_analysis: 1 × 4 ANOVAs for ROI-wise deviation score comparisons across groups (HC, SCHZ, BPD, ADHD) with FDR correction and lower-level t-tests. Binary logistic regression for classification using summary metrics with ROC curves and AUC calculation. Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests for within-group similarity distributions. Non-parametric repeated measures ANOVAs (Friedman test) with Conover post-hoc comparisons (Bonferroni corrected) for within- vs between-group similarity. Pearson correlations between transdiagnostic similarity and summary deviation metrics (Bonferroni corrected p<0.05/30). Mass univariate regression analyses (2000 permutations, FDR correction) using PALM for deviation-symptom mapping with four PCA-derived symptom components.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_brief: Transdiagnostic deviations in cholinergic and glutamatergic molecular-enriched networks mapped onto a spectrum of psychotic, depressive, inattentive, and impulsive symptoms across schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and ADHD, revealing shared neurobiological mechanisms beyond traditional diagnostic boundaries.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_findings_detailed: Normative modeling revealed significant between-group differences in VAChT (cholinergic) and mGluR5 (glutamatergic) systems. For VAChT, differences were found between HC and SCHZ in multiple regions including left putamen, left angular gyrus, bilateral precuneus, left SMA, right lobule IX, and vermal lobule VIIIb. For mGluR5, both SCHZ and BPD differed from HC, with FC values largely lower than normal ranges in vermal lobule VI and right mid-occipital cortex. Summary deviation metrics showed moderate classification capacity: mGluR5 AUC=0.75 for SCHZ, 0.66 for BPD; GABA-A AUC=0.73 for SCHZ. ADHD showed no significant differences from HC in any molecular system. PCA identified four symptom components explaining 57.3% of variance, with PC2 capturing a transdiagnostic dysregulation spectrum (psychotic, depressive, inattentive, motor impulsiveness symptoms). Transdiagnostic similarity in deviation patterns correlated negatively with summary deviation metrics for NAT, SERT, mGluR5, and GABA-A systems (Bonferroni corrected), indicating greater similarity associated with more negative deviations. PC2 scores correlated significantly with transdiagnostic similarity in SERT, VAChT, and mGluR5 systems. Mass univariate deviation-symptom mapping revealed significant relationships between PC2 and deviations in VAChT-enriched networks (bilateral insula/operculum, left mid-cingulate, SMA, precuneus) and mGluR5-enriched networks (bilateral insula/operculum, bilateral STG, bilateral cuneus, left lingual gyrus, bilateral mid-cingulate, bilateral SMA). All relationships were negative, with higher symptom scores associated with lower molecular-enriched FC than normative ranges. Sensitivity analyses showed normative modeling provided substantial advantage over conventional REACT analyses, which yielded no significant between-group differences and only limited deviation-symptom relationships.
clinical_application_and_analysis.key_limitations: Cross-sectional design limits causal inference and temporal trajectory characterization. Relatively small clinical sample sizes (38-44 per group) require replication in larger, more diverse cohorts. Patients were not drug-naive or drug-free; medication effects on molecular-enriched networks cannot be excluded. Molecular templates derived from separate healthy cohorts using different methodologies with varying resolutions. Moderate collinearity between some molecular templates (though VIF<5). Only one dataset (UCLA) tested for deviation-symptom mapping; simplified transdiagnostic symptom measures needed for replication. No treatment outcome measures available to test predictive utility. REACT does not directly measure neurotransmitter activity despite using receptor/transporter density information. Model explained variance was moderate and varied substantially across regions and systems.
clinical_application_and_analysis.application_notes: This work provides proof-of-concept for combining molecular-enriched functional imaging with normative modeling to characterize individual-level dysfunction amenable to pharmacotherapeutic intervention. The approach enables scalable characterization of molecular- and systems-level mechanisms using existing fMRI data without requiring individual PET scans. Results support emerging interest in cholinergic compounds for schizophrenia treatment (e.g., xanomeline), potentially acting through normalization of cholinergic system dysfunction. The transdiagnostic deviation-symptom mapping offers a framework for developing biomarkers that link symptom constellations to molecular circuit dysfunction across diagnostic boundaries. Future applications could include stratifying patients for targeted treatments based on molecular-enriched network deviations, testing treatment response prediction, and expanding to additional neurotransmitter receptor subtypes. The similarity-symptom and deviation-symptom approaches may form basis for novel transdiagnostic symptom-network biomarkers in precision psychiatry.

general_notes.general_notes: This is the first study to combine REACT methodology with normative modeling approaches. The study employed 28 psychometric measures across three clinical groups: Young Mania Rating Scale (YMRS), Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-17), Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale (BPRS) with subscales, Hopkins Symptom Checklist (HSCL), Adult Self-Report Scale (ASRS), Barratt Impulsiveness Scale (BIS), Scale for Traits that Increase Risk for Bipolar II Disorder (BPT), and Chapman Scale for Perceptual Aberrations (CHAP). The molecular templates used were derived from independent PET/SPECT studies: NAT from 10 HC (M/F 6/4, age 33.3±10.0) using [11C]O-methylreboxetine; DAT from 30 HC using 123I-Ioflupane SPECT; SERT from 16 HC (M/F 10/6, age 59.4±8.1) using [11C]DASB; VAChT from 6 HC (M/F 3/3, age 67.0±11.12) using 18F-fluoroethoxybenzovesamicol; GABA-A from 6 HC (all male, age 43±4) using [11C]flumazenil; mGluR5 from 31 HC (M/F 18/13, age 45.3±18.2) using [11C]ABP688. All templates were resampled to 2mm³, reference regions were replaced with minimum GM values, and values were normalized 0-1. The REACT methodology involves two-step multiple linear regression: first spatially regressing molecular templates against fMRI data to extract system-specific time series, then regressing these against voxel-wise BOLD to produce molecular-enriched FC maps. Positive values reflect stronger coupling to dominant BOLD fluctuations within receptor distribution; negative values reflect anti-correlation. CamCAN inclusion criteria excluded individuals with MMSE<24, communication difficulties, medical problems (PD, MS, cancer, stroke, epilepsy, head injury, hypertension, pregnancy, BPD, SCHZ, psychosis), mobility restrictions, substance abuse, or MRI contraindications. UCLA criteria required age 21-50, ≥8 years education, no significant medical illness, adequate cooperation, visual acuity ≥20/60, negative drug screening, not pregnant, right-handed, no head injury with LOC, no MRI contraindications. Diagnostic assessment used SCID-I supplemented by Adult ADHD Interview; interviewers required kappa≥0.75 for symptom agreement, specificity, sensitivity, and 0.85 for diagnostic accuracy. The study emphasizes moving beyond case-control paradigms toward individual-level characterization and transdiagnostic approaches aligned with Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) framework.
